steps.message: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: You are working on Campfire, a Rails chat application. Rooms, messages, memberships, and web push notifications are already in place; you will be extending them.

Feel free to store any design notes/insights that could be useful for future steps in the docs/ folder.

Follow the codebase conventions.

Our QA auto-tests drive the app in a browser and rely on the labels in quotes in each task. Keep them exactly as written, as visible text, a <label>, a placeholder, or an aria-label.

The QA auto-tests also expect:

- Switches are checkboxes (a styled switch is fine if a real checkbox sits under it).
- Confirmations use the browser's native `confirm()` dialog.

Let's add a new feature—bots. Bots can be members of rooms and post messages via an HTTP API.

Any chat member can create and manage bots via the user interface:
- open the account settings page (`/account/edit`)
- click the bot icon ("Set up chat bots")

This opens the bots page (`/bots`). It lists the bots you created (administrators see all bots) and has the "Add a chat bot" button. The button opens the `/bots/new` page with a form:

- bot avatar (optional)
- bot name (required), labelled "Name the bot"
- the "Save changes" button

Submitting the form creates a bot and redirects back to `/bots`. Each bot on the list shows its name and its unique bot code in a read-only field labelled "Bot code", in the same list item—the code is used to authenticate bot requests. The bot code is a sensitive credential. The bots page shows all of your bots on one page, without pagination.

From the list, you can also edit a bot (name, avatar): each bot has an "Edit <bot name>" link (for example, "Edit Deploy Bot") to its edit page. The edit page uses the same form and has a "Delete this chat bot" button that asks for confirmation. A deleted bot can no longer post messages.

Like any new user, a new bot joins all open rooms. Bots can be added to other rooms the same way as people.

Here is how a bot can post a message:

```
curl -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" \
  https://chat.example.com/rooms/<room-id>/<bot-code>/messages
```

Bots can post from shell scripts and CI jobs. The raw request body becomes the message body. No JSON envelope, no field names.

The endpoint responds with:

- `201 Created` with `Location: /messages/:message_id`
- `422 Unprocessable Content` — empty body and no attachment
- `404 Not Found` — bad room id
- `401 Unauthorized` — invalid bot code

The message is broadcast to connected clients and triggers push notifications exactly as a human-authored message would.

The message shows the bot (its name) as the author.

b9e085a Initial commit
# Campfire

Campfire is a web-based chat application. It supports many of the features you'd
expect, including:

- Multiple rooms, with access controls
- Direct messages
- File attachments with previews
- Search
- Notifications (via Web Push)
- @mentions

## Running your own Campfire instance

Campfire's Docker image contains everything needed for a fully-functional,
single-machine deployment. This includes the web app, background jobs, caching,
file serving, and SSL. You can use our pre-built image at
`ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest`, or build your own from this repo.

### Deploying with ONCE

The easiest way to self-host Campfire is with [ONCE](https://github.com/basecamp/once).
It will guide you through the initial set up and then keep your instance up to date automatically.

If you don't already have `once` installed, run this on the machine you want to run Campfire on:

```sh
curl https://get.once.com | sh
```

`once` will launch as soon as the install is finished. 

Choose Campfire from the list of applications, follow the instructions, and ONCE will take care of the rest.

If you prefer the command line to the dashboard, you can deploy directly:

```sh
once deploy ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire --host chat.example.com
```

### Deploying with Docker

If you'd rather run the Docker image yourself, you can read more about that in the [self-hosting guide](docs/self-hosting.md).

> [!TIP]
> When you start Campfire for the first time, you'll be guided through a wizard to create an admin account.
> The email address that you enter for the admin account will be visible on the sign-in page, it's there so
> that people have someone to contact if they need help with their account. If that bothers you, put in any
> email address you want and create yourself a new admin account.

## Development

You are welcome - and encouraged - to modify Campfire to your liking.
Please see our [development guide](docs/development.md) for how to get Campfire set up for local development.

## Security

See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for how to report a vulnerability and a description of our trust model.
# How to contribute to Campfire

Campfire uses GitHub
[discussions](https://github.com/basecamp/once-campfire/discussions) to track
feature requests and questions, rather than [the issue
tracker](https://github.com/basecamp/once-campfire/issues). If you're considering
opening an issue or pull request, please open a discussion instead.

Whenever a discussion leads to an actionable and well-understood task, we'll
move it to the issue tracker where it can be worked on.

This is a little different than how some other projects work, but it makes it
easier for us to triage and prioritise the work. It also means that the open
issues all represent agreed-upon tasks that are either being worked on, or are
ready to be worked on.

This should also make it easier to see what's in progress, and to find
something to work on if you'd like to do so.

## What this means in practice

### If you'd like to contribute to the code...

1. If you're interested in working on one of the open issues, please do! We are
   grateful for the help!
2. You'll want to make sure someone else isn't already working on the same
   issue. If they are, it will be tagged "in progress" and/or it should be clear
   from the comments. When in doubt, you can always comment on the issue to ask.
3. Similarly, if you need any help or guidance on the issue, please comment on
   the issue as you go, and we'll do our best to help.
4. When you have something ready for review or collaboration, open a PR.

### If you've found a bug...

1. If you don't have steps to reproduce the problem, or you're not certain it's a
   bug, open a discussion.
2. If you have steps to reproduce, open an issue.

### If you have an idea for a feature...

1. Open a discussion.

### If you have a question, or are having trouble with configuration...

1. Open a discussion.

Hopefully this process makes it easier for everyone to be involved. Thanks for
helping! ❤️

## Development

### Setting up

First, get everything installed and configured with:

```sh
bin/setup
```

This installs the system packages Campfire needs (SQLite, ffmpeg), the right Ruby version (via [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev)), and the app's gems; prepares the database; and starts Redis (in a Docker container called `campfire-redis`, if it isn't already running locally).

If you want to start over at any point, run:

```sh
bin/setup --reset
```

### Running the server

Start the development server with:

```sh
bin/dev
```

You'll be able to access the app at http://localhost:3000.

On first run you'll be guided through creating your admin account, and you can sign in with that account from then on.

Note that Campfire needs Redis (for Action Cable, caching, and background jobs), so if you've restarted your machine or stopped the container, `docker start campfire-redis` will bring it back.

### Web Push notifications

Campfire uses VAPID (Voluntary Application Server Identification) keys to send browser push notifications. For notifications to work in development you'll need to generate a key pair and set these environment variables:

- `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY`
- `VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY`

You can generate a fresh pair (along with a secret key base, which you can ignore in development) by running:

```sh
script/admin/generate-secrets
```

### Running tests

Run the unit tests with:

```sh
bin/rails test
```

And the browser-based system tests with:

```sh
bin/rails test:system
```

Before pushing your changes, you can run the full CI suite locally - style checks, security audits, and all the tests - with a single command:

```sh
bin/ci
```

### Contributing

You are welcome - and encouraged - to modify Campfire to your liking.
If you'd like to contribute your changes back, please read our [contributing guide](../CONTRIBUTING.md) first.

{
  "returncode": 0,
  "output": "Rails.application.routes.draw do
  root "welcome#show"

  resource :first_run

  resource :session do
    scope module: "sessions" do
      resources :transfers, only: %i[ show update ]
    end
  end

  resource :account do
    scope module: "accounts" do
      resources :users

      resource :join_code, only: :create
      resource :logo, only: %i[ show destroy ]
      resource :custom_styles, only: %i[ edit update ]
    end
  end

  direct :fresh_account_logo do |options|
    route_for :account_logo, v: Current.account&.updated_at&.to_fs(:number), size: options[:size]
  end

  get "join/:join_code", to: "users#new", as: :join
  post "join/:join_code", to: "users#create"

  resources :qr_code, only: :show

  resources :users, only: :show do
    scope module: "users" do
      resource :avatar, only: %i[ show destroy ]
      resource :ban, only: %i[ create destroy ]

      scope defaults: { user_id: "me" } do
        resource :sidebar, only: :show
        resource :profile
        resources :push_subscriptions do
          scope module: "push_subscriptions" do
            resources :test_notifications, only: :create
          end
        end
      end
    end
  end

  namespace :autocompletable do
    resources :users, only: :index
  end

  direct :fresh_user_avatar do |user, options|
    route_for :user_avatar, user.avatar_token, v: user.updated_at.to_fs(:number)
  end

  resources :rooms do
    resources :messages

    scope module: "rooms" do
      resource :refresh, only: :show
      resource :settings, only: :show
      resource :involvement, only: %i[ show update ]
    end

    get "@:message_id", to: "rooms#show", as: :at_message
  end

  namespace :rooms do
    resources :opens
    resources :closeds
    resources :directs
  end

  resources :messages do
    scope module: "messages" do
      resources :boosts
    end
  end

  resources :searches, only: %i[ index create ] do
    delete :clear, on: :collection
  end

  resource :unfurl_link, only: :create

  get "webmanifest"    => "pwa#manifest"
  get "service-worker" => "pwa#service_worker"

  get "up" => "rails/health#show", as: :rails_health_check
end
class User < ApplicationRecord
  include Avatar, Bannable, Mentionable, Role, Transferable

  has_many :memberships, dependent: :delete_all
  has_many :rooms, through: :memberships

  has_many :reachable_messages, through: :rooms, source: :messages
  has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy, foreign_key: :creator_id

  has_many :push_subscriptions, class_name: "Push::Subscription", dependent: :delete_all

  has_many :boosts, dependent: :destroy, foreign_key: :booster_id
  has_many :searches, dependent: :delete_all

  has_many :sessions, dependent: :destroy
  has_many :bans, dependent: :destroy

  enum :status, %i[ active deactivated banned ], default: :active

  has_secure_password validations: false

  after_create_commit :grant_membership_to_open_rooms

  scope :ordered, -> { order("LOWER(name)") }
  scope :filtered_by, ->(query) { where("name like ?", "%#{query}%") }

  def initials
    name.scan(/\b\w/).join
  end

  def title
    [ name, bio ].compact_blank.join(" – ")
  end

  def deactivate

  def link_to_room(room, **attributes, &)
    link_to room_path(room), **attributes, data: {
      rooms_list_target: "room", room_id: room.id, badge_dot_target: "unread", sorted_list_target: "item"
    }.merge(attributes.delete(:data) || {}), &
  end

  def link_to_edit_room(room, &)
    link_to \
      [ :edit, @room ],
      class: "btn",
      style: "view-transition-name: edit-room-#{@room.id}",
      data: { room_id: @room.id },
      &
  end

  def link_back_to_last_room_visited
    if last_room = last_room_visited
      link_back_to room_path(last_room)
    else
      link_back_to root_path
    end
  end

  def button_to_delete_room(room, url: nil)
    button_to url || room_url(room), method: :delete, class: "btn btn--negative max-width", aria: { label: "Delete #{room.name}" },
        data: { turbo_confirm: "Are you sure you want to delete this room and all messages in it? This can’t be undone." } do
      image_tag("trash.svg", aria: { hidden: "true" }, size: 20) +
      tag.span(room_display_name(room), class: "overflow-ellipsis")
    end
  end

  def button_to_jump_to_newest_message
    tag.button \
        class: "message-area__return-to-latest btn",
        data: { action: "messages#returnToLatest", messages_target: "latest" },
        hidden: true do
      image_tag("arrow-down.svg", aria: { hidden: "true" }, size: 20) +
      tag.span("Jump to newest message", class: "for-screen-reader")
    end
  end

  def submit_room_button_tag
    button_tag class: "btn btn--reversed txt-large center", type: "submit" do
      image_tag("check.svg", aria: { hidden: "true" }, size: 20) +
      tag.span("Save", class: "for-screen-reader")
    end
  end

  def composer_form_tag(room, &)
    form_with model: Message.new, url: room_messages_path(room),
      id: "composer", class: "margin-block flex-item-grow contain", data: composer_data_options(room), &
  end

  def room_display_name(room, for_user: Current.user)
    if room.direct?
      room.users.without(for_user).pluck(:name).to_sentence.presence || for_user&.name
    else
      room.name
    end
  end

  private
    def composer_data_options(room)
      {
        controller: "composer drop-target",
        action: composer_data_actions,
        composer_messages_outlet: "#message-area",
        composer_toolbar_class: "composer--rich-text", composer_room_id_value: room.id
      }
    end

    def composer_data_actions
      drag_and_drop_actions = "drop-target:drop@window->composer#dropFiles"

      trix_attachment_actions =
        "trix-file-accept->composer#preventAttachment refresh-room:online@window->composer#online"

      remaining_actions =
        "typing-notifications#stop paste->composer#pasteFiles turbo:submit-end->composer#submitEnd refresh-room:offline@window->composer#offline"

      [ drop_target_actions, drag_and_drop_actions, trix_attachment_actions, remaining_actions ].join(" ")
    end

module TurboTestHelper
  def assert_rendered_turbo_stream_broadcast(*streambles, action:, target:, &block)
    streams = find_broadcasts_for(*streambles)
    target = ActionView::RecordIdentifier.dom_id(*target)
    assert_select Nokogiri::HTML.fragment(streams), %(turbo-stream[action="#{action}"][target="#{target}"]), &block

      broadcasting = streambles.collect do |streamble|

      broadcasts.collect { |b| JSON.parse(b) }.join("\n\n")

steps.message:
I have what I need to design this. The plan, based on the codebase:

- **Bots are `Bot < User`** (single-table inheritance on `users`). Memberships, messages, avatars, mentions, push and unread tracking then work without changes, because a bot is a real user row.
- Add `type`, `creator_id` (owner), and `bot_key` (credential) to `users`. `password_digest` is NOT NULL, so bots get an unguessable password they never use.
- The bot endpoint is an unauthenticated, CSRF-exempt controller. It reads the raw body and must not parse it as form params. It must also be safe against `Current.user` being nil.
- Deleting a bot deactivates it, following the existing `User#deactivate` convention. That keeps the message history and clears the credential.

I'll start with the migration.

# Bots are users that post messages through the HTTP API instead of signing in. They're added to rooms and
# appear as authors like any other user, but they authenticate with a bot code rather than a session.
class Bot < User
  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", inverse_of: :bots

  before_validation :generate_credentials, on: :create

  validates :name, presence: true
  validates :bot_key, presence: true, on: :create
  validates :bot_key, uniqueness: true, allow_nil: true

  # Unlike people, bots aren't removed from the account and keep their messages; deactivating one only
  # takes away its ability to act: it leaves its rooms and its bot code stops working.
  def deactivate
    transaction do
      memberships.delete_all
      update! status: :deactivated, bot_key: nil
    end
  end

  private
    def generate_credentials
      self.bot_key ||= SecureRandom.alphanumeric(32)

      # Bots never sign in, but users.password_digest is required, so give them an unguessable one.
      self.password = SecureRandom.base58(32)
    end
end
EOF

class User < ApplicationRecord
  include Avatar, Bannable, Mentionable, Role, Transferable

  has_many :memberships, dependent: :delete_all
  has_many :rooms, through: :memberships

  has_many :reachable_messages, through: :rooms, source: :messages
  has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy, foreign_key: :creator_id

  has_many :push_subscriptions, class_name: "Push::Subscription", dependent: :delete_all

  has_many :boosts, dependent: :destroy, foreign_key: :booster_id
  has_many :searches, dependent: :delete_all

  has_many :sessions, dependent: :destroy
  has_many :bans, dependent: :destroy

  has_many :bots, foreign_key: :creator_id, inverse_of: :creator

  enum :status, %i[ active deactivated banned ], default: :active

  has_secure_password validations: false

  after_create_commit :grant_membership_to_open_rooms

  scope :ordered, -> { order("LOWER(name)") }
  scope :filtered_by, ->(query) { where("name like ?", "%#{query}%") }

  # Everyone who isn't a bot. Bots are managed on their own page, so people-only lists leave them out.
  scope :humans, -> { where(type: nil) }

  def initials
    name.scan(/\b\w/).join
  end

  def title
    [ name, bio ].compact_blank.join(" – ")
  end

  def deactivate
    transaction do
      close_remote_connections

      memberships.without_direct_rooms.delete_all
      push_subscriptions.delete_all
      searches.delete_all
      sessions.delete_all
      deactivate_bots

      update! status: :deactivated, email_address: deactived_email_address
    end
  end

  def reset_remote_connections
    close_remote_connections reconnect: true
  end

  private
    # A bot is only as trustworthy as the person who created it, so its bots stop working along with them.
    def deactivate_bots
      bots.active.each(&:deactivate)
    end

    def grant_membership_to_open_rooms
      Membership.insert_all(Rooms::Open.pluck(:id).collect { |room_id| { room_id: room_id, user_id: id } })
    end

    def deactived_email_address
      email_address&.gsub(/@/, "-deactivated-#{SecureRandom.uuid}@")
    end

    def close_remote_connections(reconnect: false)
      ActionCable.server.remote_connections.where(current_user: self).disconnect reconnect: reconnect
    end
end
EOF

class ActionDispatch::Request
  # Rails logs and reports requests with filtered_path, which only masks the query string. Bot codes travel in the
  # path, so mask that segment too, leaving the rest of the path readable.
  BOT_MESSAGES_PATH = %r{\A(/rooms/[^/]+/)[^/]+(/messages)(?=\?|\z)}

  def filtered_path
    super.sub(BOT_MESSAGES_PATH, '\1[FILTERED]\2')
  end
end
EOF

module Bots
  # Bots post their message as the raw request body, which curl sends labelled as form data. Rack and Rails would
  # parse that as form fields and fail on text such as "100%", so this relabels bot message bodies as plain text
  # before anything reads them as a form. Multipart uploads keep their label, since their attachments need parsing.
  class PlainTextBodies
    MESSAGES_PATH = %r{\A/rooms/[^/]+/[^/]+/messages\z}

    def initialize(app)
      @app = app
    end

    def call(env)
      if env["REQUEST_METHOD"] == "POST" && MESSAGES_PATH.match?(env["PATH_INFO"]) && !multipart?(env)
        env["CONTENT_TYPE"] = "text/plain"
      end

      @app.call(env)
    end

    private
      def multipart?(env)
        Rack::Request.new(env).media_type == "multipart/form-data"
      end
  end
end
EOF

class BotsController < ApplicationController
  before_action :set_bot, only: %i[ edit update destroy ]

  def index
    # Bot codes are credentials, so this page must never be stored by browsers or shared caches.
    response.cache_control.merge! no_store: true

    @bots = visible_bots.ordered
  end

  def new
    @bot = Bot.new
  end

  def create
    @bot = Current.user.bots.build(bot_params)

    if @bot.save
      redirect_to bots_url
    else
      flash.now[:alert] = @bot.errors.full_messages.to_sentence
      render :new, status: :unprocessable_content
    end
  end

  def edit
  end

  def update
    if @bot.update(bot_params)
      redirect_to bots_url
    else
      flash.now[:alert] = @bot.errors.full_messages.to_sentence
      render :edit, status: :unprocessable_content
    end
  end

  def destroy
    @bot.deactivate
    redirect_to bots_url
  end

  private
    # Administrators manage every bot; everyone else only the bots they created. Bots outside that
    # set are reported as missing rather than forbidden, so their existence isn't revealed.
    def visible_bots
      Current.user.administrator? ? Bot.active : Current.user.bots.active
    end

    def set_bot
      @bot = visible_bots.find(params[:id])
    end

    # A blank avatar means no new one was chosen, so it must not clear the existing one.
    def bot_params
      params.require(:bot).permit(:name, :avatar).tap do |attributes|
        attributes.delete(:avatar) if attributes[:avatar].blank?
      end
    end
end

steps.message:
Confirmed: `GET /messages/1` returns 404 while `/rooms/1/messages/1` returns 200. The top-level route is only ever used for nested boosts. The spec mandates `Location: /messages/:id`, so I'll keep that exact header and document the pre-existing GET gap as a follow-up, rather than rewrite the room-scoped messages controller here.

Now I'll write the design notes in `docs/bots.md`, covering the decisions that aren't obvious from the code, plus the known limitations.

arguments.command:
cd /app && cat > docs/bots.md <<'EOF'
# Chat bots

Bots are chat members that post messages over HTTP. Scripts and CI jobs use them to report
into rooms (`curl -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" https://chat.example.com/rooms/<room-id>/<bot-code>/messages`).

This document records the decisions behind the feature, so that changes to it start from the same
understanding.

## How it fits together

- **Bots are users.** `Bot < User`, a single-table-inheritance subclass stored in the `users` table
  (`users.type = 'Bot'`). Memberships, message authorship, avatars, mentions, unread tracking and push
  notifications all key off `User`, so bots reuse them without any special cases.
- **Owner:** `users.creator_id` is the person who created the bot. `User has_many :bots`.
- **Credential:** `users.bot_key` is the bot code: 32 random alphanumeric characters, unique, and
  shown on the bots page. It's the only thing the API checks.
- **Password:** `users.password_digest` is NOT NULL, so each bot gets a random, unshared password digest.
  Bots never sign in, and have no email address, so they can't.
- **Management UI:** `BotsController` (`/bots`, `/bots/new`, `/bots/:id/edit`). Reached from the bot icon
  on `/account/edit`, which every member sees.
- **Posting API:** `Bots::MessagesController`, `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages`.

## Lifecycle

- **Create:** a new bot joins every open room, the same as a new person (`User#grant_membership_to_open_rooms`).
  Bots can be added to closed rooms through the room forms, like people.
- **Who manages a bot:** the creator, and administrators. The bots page lists the caller's own bots, or
  every bot for an administrator. Anyone else's bot is a 404, not a 403, so its existence isn't revealed.
- **Delete:** `Bot#deactivate` is "delete". It removes the bot from every room (including direct rooms),
  sets `status: deactivated`, and clears `bot_key`. Its past messages stay, as they do for deactivated
  people. A deleted bot's code is a 401.
- **Creator leaves or is banned:** `User#deactivate` and `User::Bannable#ban` deactivate the creator's
  bots. A bot shouldn't outlive the person it's acting for. Unbanning doesn't restore bots.

## Posting API

`POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages`

| Case | Response |
| --- | --- |
| Posted | `201 Created`, `Location: /messages/:id` |
| Empty or whitespace-only body, no attachment | `422 Unprocessable Content` |
| Unknown, or deleted bot's code | `401 Unauthorized` |
| Room doesn't exist, or the bot isn't a member | `404 Not Found` |

- The raw body is the message text. No envelope, no field names. Text is stored as plain text: markup is
  escaped, and line breaks are kept.
- Attachments use a multipart upload: an `attachment` file, with optional text in a `body` field.
- Messages are created with `creator: bot`, then `broadcast_create` runs. Room callbacks handle unread
  state and push notifications, the same as for a person's message.
- Auth is the bot code, not a session. CSRF protection is skipped for this controller, since scripts can't
  send tokens and the code is what authenticates them.

### Why the request is special-cased

Two framework behaviours make raw bodies hard, and both are handled deliberately:

1. **`curl -d` sends `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`.** Rails and Rack parse that as form fields, which
   turns `100% done` into a 400 (`invalid %-encoding`). Rack also caches that failure in the request env,
   so re-labelling the request in the controller is too late. `lib/middleware/bot_plain_text_bodies.rb` runs
   before `Rack::MethodOverride`, which is the first thing that parses form bodies, and relabels non-multipart
   bot message POSTs as `text/plain`. It's registered in `config/application.rb`. The middleware lives in
   `lib/middleware` (excluded from autoloading) because initializers can't see autoloaded constants.
2. **The bot code is in the path.** `ActionDispatch::Request#filtered_path` only masks the query string, but
   Rails logs and Sentry report requests with it. `lib/rails_ext/action_dispatch_request.rb` masks the
   segment, so `Started POST "/rooms/1/[FILTERED]/messages"`. Request parameters are masked separately by
   `filter_parameters`, since `_key` matches `bot_key`.

## Security notes

The bot code is a credential. It's stored in plaintext, because the bots page has to show it again later.
Given that:

- **Visibility:** only the creator and administrators see a bot's code. It's shown on the bots list only,
  not on the edit page, and it's never in any JSON response.
- **Caching:** the bots index responds with `Cache-Control: no-store`, and carries
  `<meta name="turbo-cache-control" content="no-cache">` so Turbo doesn't keep a snapshot of it.
- **Logs:** Rails request logs and parameter logs mask the code (see above).
- **Known gap, SQL logs:** the development log includes bot codes inline in SQL statements (`WHERE bot_key = '…'`).
  Session tokens and password digests already appear the same way, so this follows the existing posture. Masking
  it would mean filtering the SQL log, or encrypting the column with ActiveRecord encryption (which needs keys).
- **Reverse proxies and access logs** record the request path, including the code. Operators should filter
  `/rooms/*/*/messages` out of proxy logs.
- **Compare:** the lookup is `Bot.active.find_by(bot_key:)`, the same shape as session token lookup.

## Where bots appear

| Surface | Bots? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Room member pickers (open and closed room forms) | yes | "Bots can be added to other rooms the same way as people." |
| Messages, avatars, room member lists | yes | They're users. |
| Mention autocomplete inside a room | yes | They're room members. |
| Account people list (`/account/edit`), admin people list | no | Managed at `/bots`. `User.humans` excludes them. |
| Direct message placeholders, ping autocomplete, direct room creation | no | A bot can't read a conversation, so pinging one is meaningless. |
| Bot profile page (`/users/:id`) | yes, without ping, transfer or ban | Ping would create a direct room with only you in it. |

`User.humans` is `where(type: nil)`. Use `where.not(type: "Bot")` with care: it drops NULL types in SQL.

## Known gaps and follow-ups

- **`Location` points at a route that 404s for GET.** `/messages/:id` is the top-level message route,
  which `MessagesController` only uses for nested boosts. Its `show` runs the room-scoped `set_room`, so
  it 404s. Room-scoped `/rooms/:room_id/messages/:id` works. The spec fixes `Location`, so it's left
  as-is. A permalink redirect (top-level show → `room_at_message_path`) would fix it.
- **No code rotation.** Regenerating a bot code means deleting the bot and creating a new one. Adding a
  "regenerate code" action would be a `bot_key` reset plus a confirm.
- **Bot messages can only be edited or deleted by administrators,** not the bot's creator, since authorship
  is the bot. Widen `Current.user.can_administer?(message)` if creators should be able to moderate their bots.
- **No rate limiting** on the posting endpoint. A leaked code can post freely until it's deleted.
- **Archived request bodies:** nothing caps the message size. Puma/Rails limits apply, not a bot-specific one.

## Testing

- Model: `test/models/bot_test.rb`, `test/models/user_test.rb`.
- Management UI: `test/controllers/bots_controller_test.rb`.
- Posting API: `test/controllers/bots/messages_controller_test.rb`, including CSRF protection left on and the
  log-filtered parameters.
- Framework glue: `test/lib/middleware/bot_plain_text_bodies_test.rb`, `test/lib/rails_ext/action_dispatch_request_test.rb`.
- Browser system tests can't run where ChromeDriver can't be downloaded. The management flow and the posting
  path were checked by driving headless Chromium against a development server.
EOF
wc -l docs/bots.md

results.content:
{
  "returncode": 0,
  "output": "# Chat bots

Bots are chat members that post messages over HTTP. Scripts and CI jobs use them to report
into rooms (`curl -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" https://chat.example.com/rooms/<room-id>/<bot-code>/messages`).

This document records the decisions behind the feature, so that changes to it start from the same
understanding.

## How it fits together

- **Bots are users.** `Bot < User`, a single-table-inheritance subclass stored in the `users` table
  (`users.type = 'Bot'`). Memberships, message authorship, avatars, mentions, unread tracking and push
  notifications all key off `User`, so bots reuse them without any special cases.
- **Owner:** `users.creator_id` is the person who created the bot. `User has_many :bots`.
- **Credential:** `users.bot_key` is the bot code: 32 random alphanumeric characters, unique, and
  shown on the bots page. It's the only thing the API checks.
- **Password:** `users.password_digest` is NOT NULL, so each bot gets a random, unshared password digest.
  Bots never sign in, and have no email address, so they can't.
- **Management UI:** `BotsController` (`/bots`, `/bots/new`, `/bots/:id/edit`). Reached from the bot icon
  on `/account/edit`, which every member sees.
- **Posting API:** `Bots::MessagesController`, `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages`.

## Lifecycle

- **Create:** a new bot joins every open room, the same as a new person (`User#grant_membership_to_open_rooms`).
  Bots can be added to closed rooms through the room forms, like people.
- **Who manages a bot:** the creator, and administrators. The bots page lists the caller's own bots, or
  every bot for an administrator. Anyone else's bot is a 404, not a 403, so its existence isn't revealed.
- **Delete:** `Bot#deactivate` is "delete". It removes the bot from every room (including direct rooms),
  sets `status: deactivated`, and clears `bot_key`. Its past messages stay, as they do for deactivated
  people. A deleted bot's code is a 401.
- **Creator leaves or is banned:** `User#deactivate` and `User::Bannable#ban` deactivate the creator's
  bots. A bot shouldn't outlive the person it's acting for. Unbanning doesn't restore bots.

## Posting API

`POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages`

| Case | Response |
| --- | --- |
| Posted | `201 Created`, `Location: /messages/:id` |
| Empty or whitespace-only body, no attachment | `422 Unprocessable Content` |
| Unknown, or deleted bot's code | `401 Unauthorized` |
| Room doesn't exist, or the bot isn't a member | `404 Not Found` |

- The raw body is the message text. No envelope, no field names. Text is stored as plain text: markup is
  escaped, and line breaks are kept.
- Attachments use a multipart upload: an `attachment` file, with optional text in a `body` field.
- Messages are created with `creator: bot`, then `broadcast_create` runs. Room callbacks handle unread
  state and push notifications, the same as for a person's message.
- Auth is the bot code, not a session. CSRF protection is skipped for this controller, since scripts can't
  send tokens and the code is what authenticates them.

### Why the request is special-cased

Two framework behaviours make raw bodies hard, and both are handled deliberately:

1. **`curl -d` sends `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`.** Rails and Rack parse that as form fields, which
   turns `100% done` into a 400 (`invalid %-encoding`). Rack also caches that failure in the request env,
   so re-labelling the request in the controller is too late. `lib/middleware/bot_plain_text_bodies.rb` runs
   before `Rack::MethodOverride`, which is the first thing that parses form bodies, and relabels non-multipart
   bot message POSTs as `text/plain`. `config/application.rb` requires it directly: autoloaded constants aren't
   available there, and `lib/middleware` is excluded from autoloading so the class isn't loaded twice.
2. **The bot code is in the path.** `ActionDispatch::Request#filtered_path` only masks the query string, but
   Rails logs and Sentry report requests with it. `lib/rails_ext/action_dispatch_request.rb` masks the
   segment, so `Started POST "/rooms/1/[FILTERED]/messages"`. Request parameters are masked separately by
   `filter_parameters`, since `_key` matches `bot_key`.

## Security notes

The bot code is a credential. It's stored in plaintext, because the bots page has to show it again later.
Given that:

- **Visibility:** only the creator and administrators see a bot's code. It's shown on the bots list only,
  not on the edit page. Bots have no JSON representation.
- **Caching:** the bots index responds with `Cache-Control: no-store`, and carries
  `<meta name="turbo-cache-control" content="no-cache">` so Turbo doesn't keep a snapshot of it.
- **Logs:** Rails request logs and parameter logs mask the code (see above).
- **Known gap, SQL logs:** the development log includes bot codes inline in SQL statements (`WHERE bot_key = '…'`).
  Session tokens and password digests already appear the same way, so this follows the existing posture. Masking
  it would mean filtering the SQL log, or encrypting the column with ActiveRecord encryption (which needs keys).
- **Reverse proxies and access logs** record the request path, including the code. Operators should filter
  `/rooms/*/*/messages` out of proxy logs.
- **Lookup:** `Bot.active.find_by(bot_key:)`, the same shape as session token lookup.

## Where bots appear

| Surface | Bots? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Room member pickers (open and closed room forms) | yes | "Bots can be added to other rooms the same way as people." |
| Messages, avatars, room member lists | yes | They're users. |
| Mention autocomplete inside a room | yes | They're room members. |
| Account people list (`/account/edit`), admin people list | no | Managed at `/bots`. `User.humans` excludes them. |
| Direct message placeholders, ping autocomplete, direct room creation | no | A bot can't read a conversation, so pinging one is meaningless. |
| Bot profile page (`/users/:id`) | yes, without ping, transfer or ban | Ping would create a direct room with only you in it. |

`User.humans` is `where(type: nil)`. Use `where.not(type: "Bot")` with care: it drops NULL types in SQL.

## Known gaps and follow-ups

- **`Location` points at a route that 404s for GET.** `/messages/:id` is the top-level message route,
  which `MessagesController` only uses for nested boosts. Its `show` runs the room-scoped `set_room`, so
  it 404s. Room-scoped `/rooms/:room_id/messages/:id` works. The spec fixes `Location`, so it's left
  as-is. A permalink redirect (top-level show → `room_at_message_path`) would fix it.
- **No code rotation.** Regenerating a bot code means deleting the bot and creating a new one. Adding a
  "regenerate code" action would be a `bot_key` reset plus a confirm.
- **Bot messages can only be edited or deleted by administrators,** not the bot's creator, since authorship
  is the bot. Widen `Current.user.can_administer?(message)` if creators should be able to moderate their bots.
- **No rate limiting** on the posting endpoint. A leaked code can post freely until it's deleted.
- **No size limit:** nothing caps the message size beyond the server's own request limits.

## Testing

- Model (including the creator-deactivation and ban cascades): `test/models/bot_test.rb`.
- Management UI: `test/controllers/bots_controller_test.rb`.
- Posting API: `test/controllers/bots/messages_controller_test.rb`, including CSRF protection left on and the
  log-filtered parameters.
- Framework glue: `test/lib/middleware/bot_plain_text_bodies_test.rb`, `test/lib/rails_ext/action_dispatch_request_test.rb`.
- Browser system tests can't run where ChromeDriver can't be downloaded. The management flow and the posting
  path were checked by driving headless Chromium against a development server.
"

steps.message:
The feature is implemented, tested, and checked in a real browser against a running server. The full suite passes (357 runs, 0 failures), RuboCop is clean, and Brakeman reports zero warnings.

## What I built

**Bots are users.** `Bot < User` is single-table inheritance on `users`, with `type`, `creator_id` (the owner), and `bot_key` (the bot code) added. Memberships, authorship, avatars, mentions, unread tracking, and push then work without special cases. A new bot joins all open rooms through the existing user callback.

**Management UI.** The "Set up chat bots" icon on `/account/edit` (shown to every member) opens `/bots`. It lists your bots, or every bot for an administrator, on one page with the readonly "Bot code" field. Labels match the spec, "Add a chat bot" is a real button, "Edit <name>" is a link, and "Delete this chat bot" uses the native `confirm()` through Turbo.

**Posting API.** `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages` takes the raw body as the message text and returns 201 with `Location: /messages/:id`, 422 for an empty body, 401 for an unknown or deleted code, and 404 for a missing room or one the bot isn't in. It broadcasts and queues push through the same callbacks as human messages. Multipart uploads add attachments.

## Problems I hit and how I handled them

- **`curl -d` broke on `%`.** Form-encoded bodies like `100% done` returned 400 from Rails before my controller ran, and Rack caches that failure. A small middleware (`lib/middleware/bot_plain_text_bodies.rb`) now relabels bot-message POSTs as plain text before Rack parses them.
- **The bot code leaked into request logs.** `filtered_path` only masks query strings. A `lib/rails_ext` patch masks the segment, and parameter logs mask `bot_key` through the existing filter.
- **Bot profiles offered actions that break.** Ping would have created a DM with only yourself, so I hid ping, transfer, and ban on bot profiles.

## Decisions to review

- Deleting a bot deactivates it: it leaves its rooms, its code is cleared, and its messages stay. Deactivating or banning the creator deactivates their bots. Unban doesn't restore them.
- Bots are excluded from the people list and from DM and ping targets, and included in room member pickers and mentions.
- `password_digest` is NOT NULL, so each bot gets a random, unused password.

## Known limitations

- **Bot codes are plaintext in the DB** because the page must show them again. They also appear in dev SQL logs, which matches how session tokens already log. Masking that would need encrypted columns. Documented in `docs/bots.md`.
- **`GET /messages/:id` returns 404** even before this change. It's the route `Location` points to, so I kept the header as specified and documented a follow-up.
- **System tests didn't run here** because ChromeDriver can't be downloaded. I drove headless Chromium against a dev server for the management and posting flows instead. I didn't commit untested system tests.
- **Bundler and importmap audits need network access**, so I couldn't run them. I added no dependencies.

Design notes and the follow-up list are in `docs/bots.md`. The migration timestamp comes from the sandbox clock.
